By twelve she had supper on the stove and her little brother's homework checked, and nobody in that house ever had to ask — being the one who never needed anything was simply her place in it. Good was expected rather than celebrated, and her grandmother calling her 'the little mother' was the highest praise she got. She grew into an adult who met every bar set for her and never once counted meeting it as having done well.

Precipitating. Four months ago the duplex she and Jesse had rented for six years was sold out from under them — the new owner wanted the unit for family, and thirty days' notice was all the law required. Nothing they could afford in town came without first, last, and a deposit they didn't have, six weeks in an extended-stay motel ate most of what savings remained, and since spring they have been in his mother's spare room. Tatiana withdrew from the evening class she had finally enrolled in at the community college, put the sewing machine and her fabric stash into a storage unit, left her flowerpots with a neighbor, and stopped staying after church for coffee. She hasn't missed a day of work, but she cried in the supply room once, and twice now she has caught mistakes in the office schedule that she would never have made before.

Protective. She still has her pew on Sunday mornings and her Thursday evening shift organizing the senior lunches at the community center, and the people there would show up for her if she ever let them — Miss Earline has already offered the church's emergency fund twice. She is still, by everyone's account including her own, very good at her job: she can soothe an angry caller and untangle a double-booked schedule without breaking stride, and she trusts that about herself even now.
